name: coacd
desc: Approximate convex decomposition for 3D meshes with collision-aware concavity
why: Approximate convex decomposition of 3D meshes, a real computational geometry idea you can run on your own models.

brief.what_it_is: CoACD is an approximate convex decomposition tool for 3D meshes. It takes a triangle mesh (the README asks for .obj input, and says the input must be triangles, not quads or n-gons) and splits it into a set of convex pieces. Each piece is a convex hull, and the set can serve as collision shapes in physics or game engines. Output goes to .obj and .wrl files, and the Python API returns a list of convex hulls. It ships as a Python package (pip install coacd), a C++ command-line binary built from source, and a Unity package.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as making geometry algorithms that only work on convex shapes, such as collision detection, usable on arbitrary meshes. It says the method preserves the collision behaviour of the input with fewer components, so it supports object interaction in downstream applications.
brief.how_it_works: The README gives little internals beyond the title, which describes a collision-aware concavity measure and a tree search (MCTS) over cutting strategies. Non-manifold inputs are first preprocessed into a watertight mesh (controlled by -pr and -pm). The decomposition then stops once the concavity falls below the threshold (-t), with an optional merge pass to reduce the piece count. The algorithm is stochastic, so results depend on --seed. The paper is linked for detail.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install, the README covers several routes. Python is pip install coacd, with Linux x86_64, Windows amd64, and macOS (x86_64 and Apple silicon) supported. For a C++ build you need git and cmake >= 3.24, with g++ 9 to below 12 on Linux, clang on macOS 10.14+, and MSVC 2019/2022 on Windows. Parallelism uses OpenMP by default on Linux and Windows, and off by default on macOS. Unity 2020.1 or later is installed by adding the package from the git URL https://github.com/SarahWeiii/CoACD.git?path=/Packages/info.flandre.coacd#unity through the Package Manager. The README does not mention accounts, GPUs, or licence keys for the core tool.
brief.standout: Collision-aware concavity: the cuts are chosen to keep collision behaviour, not just to minimise geometric error, and the tree search over cut strategies is a deliberate step beyond greedy splitting. It also has a real-metric mode (-rm) that takes the threshold in meters, and a --split option that writes each part to its own file so engines like MuJoCo or Bullet don't collapse the parts back into one convex shape.
brief.status: maintained. The README has news items dated 2023-06, 2023-10, 2025-09, 2026-04, and 2026-09, and a build badge. It points to a successor library, CuACD, announced in 2026-09 as a GPU-resident implementation of the same lookahead-search formulation. I did not see a release date or last-commit date on the page itself.
brief.caveats: The input must be a triangle mesh. Non-manifold inputs go through a preprocessing step that can change the geometry, and turning it off with -pm off can crash or give wrong results unless the mesh is 2-manifold. The default parameters are the fast setting, so better results cost more runtime. -c max hull counts can produce hulls whose concavity exceeds the threshold. Building from source has compiler version limits, and the Windows build needs specific MSVC flags. The README's news points to CuACD as a faster alternative, which may matter for batch use. The Unity path is documented only for the Unity branch and the git-URL install.
quotes: Approximate convex decomposition enables efficient geometry processing algorithms specifically designed for convex shapes (e.g., collision detection).
In most cases, you only need to adjust the `threshold` (0.01~1) to balance the level of detail and the number of decomposed components.
`--seed` is used for reproduction of the same results as our algorithm is stochastic.
